Hybrid Time Series Models for Short-Term Sea-Level Forecasting
papers.abstract: Accurate tide forecasts are essential for coastal management, navigation, flood-risk reduction, and infrastructure protection. Observed sea level can be decomposed into astronomical and non-astronomical components, the latter mainly driven by meteorological effects. This study investigates a hybrid framework for hourly sea-level forecasting that combines harmonic analysis (HA) for the astronomical component with data-driven models for the non-astronomical contribution. The approach is evaluated at six tide-gauge stations with different tidal regimes: Venice, Trieste, Saint-Malo, Vard{\o}, Nikiski, and Nagasaki. Four data-driven model classes are considered: (i) autoregressive and (ii) functional autoregressive models with exogenous variables; (iii) generalized additive models and autoregressive neural networks; and (iv) a novel semi-functional k-nearest-neighbours approach that combines similarity in recent non-astronomical trajectories and meteorological conditions. Point forecasts are complemented by upper quantile forecasts, obtained by historical simulation of out-of-sample errors, targeting the right tail of the sea-level distribution. At the 24-hour horizon, hybrid models reduce the mean absolute and root mean squared errors of HA by 54.9% and 52.9% on average, while the best hybrid model reduces the HA quantile score by 40--60%. HA systematically underestimates the right tail. No hybrid specification dominates across locations, although the generalized additive model is the most competitive overall. For Venice, replacing observed meteorological covariates with operational Global Forecast System weather forecasts leaves 24- and 48-hour accuracy virtually unchanged. A cost--loss analysis of the MoSE flood-barrier system, based on these real-time forecasts, shows that hybrid forecasts substantially reduce decision losses relative to HA.

Assimilation of Velocity Data for Tidal Hydrodynamics Model Calibration
papers.venue: Journal of Advances in Modeling Earth Systems
papers.abstract: Assessing tidal stream energy resource typically involves the application of numerical models calibrated against sparse Acoustic Doppler Current Profiler (ADCP) data. This introduces significant challenges in energetic sites which are prone to significant spatiotemporal variations, like the Pentland Firth, Scotland, which is home to the world's highest capacity commercial tidal array. This study investigates the implications of limited calibration data and examines different approaches for constructing an appropriate friction field in tidal hydrodynamics model calibration. We compare performances between models using uniform and sediment‐based friction coefficient fields and introduce the first application of adjoint‐based calibration for optimizing a resource assessment model based on velocity data. The adjoint approach is applied iteratively and adjusts the friction coefficient with successive ADCP surveys. Our results demonstrate that the most widely applied approach employing a uniform friction coefficient fails to deliver adequate predictive performance across multiple data sets, even at close proximity. In turn, initial adjoint‐based calibrations are prone to overfitting, which is rectified only with additional data acquisition. Simultaneously, calibration to solely the channel of interest could lead to significant inaccuracy in kinetic energy fluxes and thus greatly impact upper bound estimates on the resource and array‐array interactions. These findings highlight the critical need for extensive and strategic ADCP data collection, which significantly reduces uncertainty and enhances model reliability, advancing the fidelity of coastal ocean models as in the tidal energy application we consider in this study.

papers.title: NLT-Net: Deep Sparse Regression with Nonlinear Loss Transformation for Automated Equation Discovery
UNIDE: Cross-PDE Learning for Noise-Robust Discovery of Governing Equations
papers.abstract: Governing partial differential equations (PDEs) provide compact and interpretable descriptions of physical systems. Classical methods, such as sparse and symbolic regression, fit a new equation to each observed field: what is learned on one system is not carried to the next, and observation noise corrupts the derivative features they rely on. This paper introduces UNIDE (Unified Identification of Differential Equations), a data-driven approach that learns across PDE families to identify governing equations from new noisy trajectories. It integrates three components: a self-supervised denoiser trained without clean targets, an encoder shared across PDE families that predicts which candidate terms are active, and weak-form least squares with residual-based pruning that estimates their coefficients. We demonstrate UNIDE on synthetic one-dimensional trajectories from six PDE families with known term structures, including the Burgers and Kuramoto--Sivashinsky equations. We train one model per noise level and systematically compare UNIDE with SINDy, WSINDy, and PySR. The results show that UNIDE recovers the exact set of governing terms more often than all three at every noise level from $1\%$ to $80\%$. At $80\%$ noise, where the noise standard deviation is $0.8$ times that of the field, it recovers the exact terms for $92\%$ of held-out trajectories, whereas the best baseline recovers about $1\%$. UNIDE is also efficient: because its neural components are reused rather than refit, it identifies each new trajectory in $0.45$ seconds, $2.7$ times faster than WSINDy and $51$ times faster than PySR. These results demonstrate the potential of learning across PDE families for efficient equation identification under substantial observation noise.

papers.title: Discovering like a scientist: Literature-informed dimensionless learning for physical closure of data-driven equations
papers.abstract: Data-driven methods can recover compact equations, yet the physical dependence of their coefficients across operating conditions often remains unresolved. Dimensionless groups can explain this variation, but selecting relevant groups from the many dimensionally admissible combinations remains challenging. Here, we introduce a knowledge-guided framework for dimensionless learning, called {\pi}-former. It learns patterns of variable association and exponent assignment from a corpus of 1,288 established dimensionless groups. Under exact dimensional constraints, the model proposes interpretable basic groups whose combinations are optimized against observations. Across seven physical problems, the framework identifies predictive dimensionless coordinates within seconds. Integration with equation discovery further expresses condition-dependent coefficients through these coordinates, recovering established physical scalings in multi-condition simulations. Applied to experimental measurements of evaporation-driven wetting, the framework discovers dimensionless coordinates and uses them to construct a unified trajectory equation. The resulting model generalizes to held-out conditions across liquids and initial volumes, outperforming existing empirical models. These results establish dimensionless learning as a transferable bridge between accumulated scientific knowledge and data-driven equation discovery, enabling artificial intelligence to uncover physically meaningful laws from observations.

papers.title: LegoSR: A Unified Framework for Self-Improving Agent-Guided Scientific Discovery
papers.abstract: Discovering equations from data provides governing laws, constitutive relations and closure models for scientific understanding and prediction. Yet a method that succeeds on one system may fail on another or on noisy data, so discovery depends on expert trial and error. Unsuccessful searches can still reveal useful parts of an equation, but these clues must be recognized and combined. We present LegoSR, a unified framework for agent-guided equation discovery built on composable discovery and cumulative experience. Seven complementary equation discovery methods and shared computational modules form reusable building blocks, connected through a common equation representation. Researchers can launch discovery with one command and guide it with partially known equations. LegoSR Agent selects methods, revises searches using feedback and combines partial findings into new hypotheses. Its Experience Library consolidates graded outcomes into lessons that guide later tasks across equation families. Evaluation covers 134 algebraic regression problems, 40 ordinary differential equation targets and 25 partial differential equation problems at several noise levels, together with three case studies. On noisy PDEs, LegoSR Agent recovers more equations than seven expert-tuned methods combined and stays close to them on ODEs. It also exceeds a generic agent with the same model, tools and budget by up to 28 percentage points, with 63-73% shorter median wall-clock time on PDE problems.

papers.title: Spanwise flow correction model for blade element theory considering geometric effects by symbolic regression
papers.abstract: Abstract Content of image described in text. The finite span and twist of wind turbine blades induce spanwise flow, along with a tip vortex. Conventional blade element theory, rooted in a two-dimensional assumption, cannot capture these spanwise effects. However, most existing three-dimensional (3-D) corrections neglect intrinsic geometric effects leading to inaccuracies near the tip and in non-rotating cases. To address this, we propose the 3-D geometric effects model incorporating axial and radial velocity factors (3-DGAR model), a physically consistent correction to blade element momentum theory. The model captures two fundamental phenomena: downwash that modifies the local effective angle of attack and tip pressure loss driven by radial velocity transport. A coherent physical pathway from the tip vortex to load reduction is established: the spanwise flow transports energy from the tip element into the tip vortex, reducing suction-side velocity and thereby weakening suction at the equivalent angle of attack. Furthermore, symbolic regression is then used to determine two unknown velocity factors from limited experimental data, serving as closure terms. The model identifies the local aspect ratio as a key parameter governing downwash and reveals an exponential decay of tip-loss effects along the span. Validation across blades of varying geometries and operating conditions confirms accurate spanwise flow correction. The results establish a clear link between the correction factors and the underlying flow physics, thereby connecting aerodynamic predictions to flow mechanisms. Overall, the 3-DGAR model provides a functional mapping from geometric inputs to aerodynamic loads, ensuring broad applicability across diverse blade designs.

See, Hypothesize, Validate: Multimodal Agentic Framework for Discovering Governing PDEs
papers.abstract: Discovering governing partial differential equations (PDEs) from observational data remains a core challenge across the sciences. Existing sparse-regression, symbolic-regression, and LLM-based approaches can be constrained by predefined libraries, noise sensitivity, hallucination, or limited iterative refinement. We introduce \textbf{MAGE} (\textbf{M}ultimodal \textbf{A}gentic \textbf{G}overning \textbf{E}quation Discovery), an agentic framework that organizes PDE discovery as a \textit{confidence governed hypothesis validation loop} inspired by the scientific cycle of observation, hypothesis, and falsification. Four role-specialized agents collaborate: a \textit{Differential Observer} computing derivatives and diagnostic visualizations; a VLM-powered \textit{Phenomenology Extractor} distilling qualitative cues from multimodal diagnostics; an LLM-driven \textit{Governing Law Synthesizer} proposing candidates without a predefined library; and an \textit{Equation Arbiter} fitting coefficients and assigning confidence scores. Discovery iterates until the top candidate clears a user-specified threshold, providing a structured process with an explicit accept-reject protocol. On the evaluated canonical PDE suite, MAGE obtains \textbf{8/8} exact structural recovery and the lowest coefficient error among the compared methods on \textbf{7/8} systems, with improvements of up to \textbf{4 orders of magnitude} and a geometric-mean improvement of approximately \textbf{3 orders of magnitude}. The pipeline also recovers the expected operators in two complex geometries and, on one laboratory sensor record, selects a cubic restoring-force model with held-out $R^2=0.98538$. These results support further study of structured agentic reasoning for library-free governing-law discovery, while broader generalization remains to be evaluated.

papers.title: Hypothesize, Evaluate, Refine: A Scientific Agent for PDE Discovery with Unknown Spatial Coefficient Fields
papers.abstract: Discovering PDEs in heterogeneous media requires jointly identifying the governing operator and the unknown spatial fields that parameterize it. These tasks are coupled: changing field placement changes the differential law, while a sufficiently flexible field can conceal structural error on a single trajectory. We present Hypothesize, Evaluate, Refine for PDE Discovery (HER-PDE), a scientific-agent framework that discovers compositional PDE structure together with nonparametric, time-invariant coefficient fields. The Agent analyzes two noisy trajectories generated by different excitations, proposes complete expression-tree hypotheses, and combines creative structural exploration with local candidate refinement. Its Hypothesis Evaluation Interface (HEI) estimates only the fields explicitly declared in each hypothesis, never adds missing terms, and scores structures by bidirectional cross-excitation transfer. The selected law is subsequently audited on a sealed temporal interval. Across five controlled two-dimensional systems observed with 5 percent relative Gaussian state noise, the Agent recovers the generating operator in all five cases, including equivalent signed-field and product-rule parameterizations. Across nine unknown coefficient fields, the recovered fields attain a median Pearson correlation of approximately 0.85 and a median relative L2 error of approximately 0.28. These results show that agent-guided hypothesis refinement can recover heterogeneous governing laws without prescribing a parametric form for their spatial coefficients.

papers.title: Large language models for partial differential equation workflows
papers.abstract: Numerical methods and deep learning have advanced the modelling and simulation of systems governed by partial differential equations (PDEs), while formulating equations, configuring solvers, and translating simulations into design and control decisions continue to demand substantial domain expertise and computational resources. Large language models (LLMs) offer opportunities to automate and coordinate these tasks by combining scientific knowledge, mathematical reasoning, code generation, and tool use. Here we review LLM-assisted PDE research across three stages, including discovery, solving, and optimization. We examine how LLMs interact with physical knowledge, numerical methods, and computational feedback to formulate models, implement solution procedures, and guide design and control. We also review existing benchmarks and evaluation practices for assessing scientific validity, computational performance, and workflow reliability. Finally, we discuss three interconnected challenges and opportunities: developing mathematical and physical reasoning tailored to specific PDE problems; building transferable domain expertise through domain-specific and multimodal post-training; and integrating active experimental design with scientific validation for open-ended problems. These directions outline a path towards a more substantive role for LLMs in developing and testing scientific ideas and computational methods across PDE research.

papers.title: Robust Symbolic PDE Discovery via Context-Aware Attention Neural Field and Uncertainty-Weighted Regression
Freeze, Then Select: Structured Field Adapters and Stability-Validated Weak Selection for PDE Discovery from Sparse Observations
papers.abstract: PDE discovery from sparse observations requires reconstructing a continuous field and selecting the correct differential terms. Our analysis of optimization paths in coupled neural PDE discovery reveals three behaviors: the exact support can persist to the end of training, appear only transiently, or fail to emerge. To decouple equation selection from neural optimization, we develop a freeze-then-select method combining a structured field adapter with Stability-Validated Weak Selection (SVWS). Trained from observations without a PDE residual, the adapter factorizes the field into learned spatial features and temporal coefficients represented by cubic splines. After freezing the field, SVWS identifies recurrent terms across independent weak-form systems, refits candidate supports, and selects the final equation on held-out weak-form systems. Beyond fixed libraries, we apply the same principle to expressions generated by genetic programming and recover the power-law form of an unknown nonlinear diffusion function from sparse, noisy observations. Across all six sparse MDBench regimes, our method attains the highest exact support recovery rate, with its clearest gains over classical and neural baselines on challenging Kuramoto-Sivashinsky dynamics.

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence for Atmospheric and Oceanic Forecasting and Research: A Fudan University Perspective
On the post-hoc Evaluation of PDE Discovery: A Multifaceted Challenge of Scientific Advancement
papers.abstract: PDE discovery aims to identify from data the governing law of a physical system. Constituting a cornerstone of scientific advancement, it has become during the past decade a major line of research in the rapidly evolving field of Physics-informed Machine Learning (PiML). Among the open problems to address in this domain, the post-hoc evaluation of discovered PDEs raises the particular difficulty of being multifaceted. Indeed, it requires jointly considering predictive accuracy, physical consistency, interpretability, and out-of-distribution generalization capacity, some of these properties being conflicting. Drawing on an extensive body of literature spanning ML, numerical analysis and symbolic regression, we establish in this article that the overwhelming majority of papers address only certain aspects of the overall evaluation task. To better understand their limitations when used in isolation from the others, we propose the first taxonomy of PDE evaluation metrics. Through experiments conducted on several PDEs, we observe that limiting the scope of the evaluation can lead to overstated conclusions as well as changes in the ranking of the identified equations. For this reason, we provide recommendations with the aim of promoting standardized and reliable practices. This results in Pde-Check, a simple rules-based protocol to guide practitioners according to the scenario under consideration, including whether or not the ground truth equation is available (recovery or discovery), whether data is available beyond the training time frame and/or under varying initial conditions, or whether physical priors is available. We argue that this paper is intended both for ML experts who design new PDE discovery algorithms and for users of these methods aiming, in real applications, to discover and validate well-founded scientific laws.and validate well-founded scientific laws.

papers.venue: Afyon Kocatepe University Journal of Sciences and Engineering
papers.abstract: Bu çalışmada, genelleştirilmiş sığ su benzeri denklem için Modifiye Basit Denklem (MSE) ve Exp-Φ(ζ) yöntemleri kullanılarak yeni tam çözümler elde edilmiştir. Ele alınan denklem, değişen fiziksel koşullar altında sığ su dalgalarının karmaşık davranışlarını tanımlayan, akışkanlar dinamiğinde önemli bir doğrusal olmayan modeldir. MSE ve Exp-Φ(ζ) yöntemleri, doğrusal olmayan kısmi diferansiyel denklemlerin analitik çözümlerinin elde edilmesinde etkili ve kullanışlı tekniklerdir. Bu yöntemler kullanılarak elde edilen sonuçlar, genelleştirilmiş sığ su benzeri denklem için farklı çözüm yapılarının ortaya konulmasını sağlamış ve bu yöntemlerin doğrusal olmayan dalga modellerinin analizinde güvenilir araçlar olduğunu göstermiştir.

Reproduction of critical wave events for the design of floating offshore structures
papers.abstract: This work presents a methodology for identifying and reproducing critical wave events that induce extreme mooring line tension in floating offshore wind turbines. The approach begins with fully non-linear sea-state realisations, generated using a JONSWAP spectrum and propagated via a fully non-linear potential flow solver. The Hilbert transform is applied on the linear component obtained from a four-wave spectral decomposition process of the surface elevation, to extract amplitude envelopes and instantaneous phase information, enabling the isolation of critical wave events responsible for extreme structural responses. Each critical wave event is expressed as a sum of focused wave groups using a Gaussian envelope regression methodology, allowing for individual iterative amplitude correction and phase focusing to overcome the challenges of reproducing steep wave events. The corrected focused wave groups are then recombined to create a ‘Hyper-Group’ with accurate spatial and temporal focusing at the desired location. The reproduced event is numerically validated against the original sea-state, demonstrating very good agreement in induced mooring line tension. This methodology provides an efficient framework for generating realistic design waves, supporting targeted numerical and experimental testing of floating offshore wind turbines under extreme conditions.

Numerical Study on the Evolution of Peregrine Breathers in Variable Depths
papers.venue: Journal of Marine Science and Engineering
papers.abstract: The Peregrine breather (PB), a classical localized solution of the nonlinear Schrödinger equation (NLSE), is widely used to describe the evolution of deep-water rogue waves. However, the influence of variable bathymetry on PB focusing remains insufficiently understood. A two-dimensional RANS–VOF numerical wave tank is therefore established using computational fluid dynamics (CFD) to investigate deterministic PB propagation over variable bathymetry. The model is validated through mesh- and time-step-sensitivity analyses and comparison with the analytical PB solution. Relative water depth, bathymetric interaction length, and bathymetric position are systematically examined. The results reveal for the first time a bathymetry-induced delayed-focusing phenomenon: the PB undergoes local defocusing over elevated topography and refocuses farther downstream after re-entering deeper water. The delay increases as water depth decreases. For k0hshelf > 1.363, increasing the interaction length mainly enhances the focusing delay, while self-focusing recovers in deeper water. In contrast, for k0hshelf < 1.363, an interaction length of approximately two carrier wavelengths disrupts the coherent PB structure and splits it into two wave packets. The onset position of bathymetric forcing has only a minor effect on the final delay. These results clarify how variable bathymetry modulates PB focusing and structural stability and provide a theoretical reference for nearshore extreme-wave risk assessment.

On Modelling the Scattering of Highly Nonlinear Transient Water Waves Due to Surface-Piercing Cylinder. Part I: Formulations and Verifications
papers.abstract: The presence of extreme ocean waves poses substantial threats to the safety of marine engineering applications and navigational activities. Accurate prediction of the nonlinear wave loads on offshore structures in large-diameter cylindrical configuration, such as monopile wind turbines and platform columns, requires a robust solution to the high-order wave diffraction problem. This paper introduces a novel, highly nonlinear time-domain numerical pseudo-spectrum model based on potential flow theory. By leveraging the Fredholm integral equation of the second kind and Legendre polynomials, a distinct efficient solver for computing the velocity potential on the cylinder surface and vertical velocity at free surface is developed. The present method is verified by comparing with a direct approach based on Fourier transform and established theoretical models for simulating the scattering of small steepness uniform waves. The convergence and computational efficiency of the present method is also demonstrated. The validation of the new model for simulating highly nonlinear transient water waves will be reported in Part II. The proposed model provides a powerful and efficient new framework for analyzing high-order nonlinear wave diffraction and hydrodynamic loads, with significant implications for both scientific research and the engineering design of coastal and offshore structures.

Attenuation of shoaling extreme wave crests by artificial salt marshes
papers.abstract: Laboratory experiments in a wave flume investigated the attenuation of shoaling extreme waves by artificial salt marshes placed immediately before an abrupt depth transition. Increasing vegetation density systematically reduced the excess kurtosis of the surface elevation distribution in the intermediate water depth regime. Nonetheless, attenuation exhibits a short saturation regime at low vegetation densities, whereas at very high densities, excess kurtosis decreases significantly across the gauges. However, kurtosis attenuation becomes ineffective as waves approach shallow-water conditions or as second-order nonlinear effects become significant. Furthermore, the highest experimental densities where the kurtosis is tamed exceed typical natural salt marsh stem densities. Thus, in natural settings, salt marshes are likely to provide only partial mitigation of extreme wave statistics in intermediate and shallow water depths, as the wave field retains some hazardous nonlinearity.

Beach scale tidal variations observed from satellite-derived shoreline time series
papers.abstract: Coastal tidal dynamics play a crucial role in a variety of biogeophysical processes, ranging from compound flooding to sediment transport. Satellite altimetry has revolutionized our understanding of ocean tides, but coastal regions remain challenging for satellite altimetry-based observations. In recent years, important efforts have been made to produce shoreline measurements from satellite optical imagery. These datasets raise the question of whether shoreline observations can resolve tidal dynamics at fine coastal scales. Here, we show that shoreline measurements provide fine-scale insights into tidal characteristics, demonstrating variability at beach scales across the Pacific Rim. We explore how both harmonic analysis and response-based methods can be applied to these data to study a range of tidal constituents. Our results are contrasted with in situ measurements and state-of-the-art models as well as with wide-swath satellite observations. We demonstrate that satellite-derived shoreline measurements are a valuable resource for tidal research, particularly for model validation and the study of tidal constituent variability in the coastal zone. Satellite-derived shoreline measurements can provide insights into coastal tidal dynamics and for the validation of models in the coastal zone, according to analyses using shoreline position data from around the Pacific Rim.

Direct spectral-inversion reconstruction of focused waves on sheared currents for cylinder-load prediction
papers.abstract: Predicting the load of a focused wave group on a cylinder in a vertically sheared current requires the incident field to reproduce the focal crest, the current-dependent propagation, and the subsurface kinematics together. Existing wave-on-current focusing relies on four-phase harmonic decomposition, which needs a linearized target spectrum and four realizations per correction. We develop a direct spectral-inversion iteration for reduced-data cases with only an event-centred free-surface segment at one gauge. The target and simulated segments are projected onto a common complex spectrum, and inlet amplitude and phase are corrected using the amplitude ratio and wrapped phase error, with one numerical realization per iteration. A four-step procedure assesses current maintenance, focal-event reconstruction, unfitted subsurface velocities with two- to three-dimensional transfer, and the inertia-dominated cylinder load under no, adverse, and following currents. In the no-current example, five iterations reduce the focus-point root mean square error from 6.4599×10−3 to 4.2769×10−3 m and raise the correlation from 0.9679 to 0.9857. Peak-load errors remain within 8.79%, with focus-window root mean square errors of 1.82–3.19 N. The inlet phase corrections follow the shear-modified dispersion, with opposite signs for adverse and following currents. The only substantial discrepancy, the following-current post-focus force, is associated with an amplitude-dominated residual in the primary and sum-frequency bands that this current carries into the post-focus window, where it acts through pressure; viscous and difference-frequency contributions are negligible. Additional no-current Joint-North-Sea-Wave-Project and Pierson–Moskowitz cases indicate portability to other unimodal spectra. Control of post-focus higher-harmonic content still requires phase decomposition.

papers.title: Third-order first-harmonic radiation by a semi-immersed sphere in forced heave motion
papers.abstract: Abstract Content of image described in text. Nonlinear hydrodynamic effects influence the power capture of resonant wave energy converters (WECs), particularly within the frequency band where these devices are designed to operate. In this study, wave flume experiments are conducted on a semi-immersed spherical model with prescribed heave motions, emulating the response to an incident broad-banded wave group. Several body motion amplitudes (up to a maximum displacement of greater than half the radius) are tested at different peak frequencies, revealing progressive reductions in both the first-harmonic radiation forces and radiated wave elevations, per unit motion amplitude, as the motion amplitude is increased. A simple partially nonlinear potential flow model incorporating instantaneous ‘volume flow’ corrections shows very good agreement with the measured radiated waves, capturing the dominant nonlinear trends. An experimental decomposition of the radiated field into channel modes is also performed, based on linear theory while accounting for linear viscous dissipation. This is then used to calculate the power in the radiated field compared to the input power from the moving body over a frequency band of interest. The model and experiments show a consistent, monotonic decrease in normalised radiated power as the amplitude of body motion increases. Overall, the findings indicate that linear theory is remarkably accurate even for quite large body motions. The most important nonlinear corrections in the first-harmonic frequency range arise from third-order potential flow interactions, fundamentally caused by the spherical geometry, and demonstrate the potential utility of volume flow models for assessing WEC radiation.

papers.abstract: Abstract Content of image described in text. Nonlinear hydrodynamic effects influence the power capture of resonant wave energy converters (WECs), particularly within the frequency band where these devices are designed to operate. In this study, wave flume experiments are conducted on a semi-immersed spherical model with prescribed heave motions, emulating the response to an incident broad-banded wave group. Several body motion amplitudes (up to a maximum displacement of greater than half the radius) are tested at different peak frequencies, revealing progressive reductions in both the first-harmonic radiation forces and radiated wave elevations, per unit motion amplitude, as the motion amplitude is increased. A simple partially nonlinear potential flow model incorporating instantaneous ‘volume flow’ corrections shows very good agreement with the measured radiated waves, capturing the dominant nonlinear trends. An experimental decomposition of the radiated field into channel modes is also performed, based on linear theory while accounting for linear viscous dissipation. This is then used to calculate the power in the radiated field compared to the input power from the moving body over a frequency band of interest. The model and experiments show a consistent, monotonic decrease in normalised radiated power as the amplitude of body motion increases. Overall, the findings indicate that linear theory is remarkably accurate even for quite large body motions. The most important nonlinear corrections in the first-harmonic frequency range arise from third-order potential flow interactions, fundamentally caused by the spherical geometry, and demonstrate the potential utility of volume flow models for assessing WEC radiation.

papers.title: Reproduction of critical wave events for the design of floating offshore structures
papers.abstract: This work presents a methodology for identifying and reproducing critical wave events that induce extreme mooring line tension in floating offshore wind turbines. The approach begins with fully non-linear sea-state realisations, generated using a JONSWAP spectrum and propagated via a fully non-linear potential flow solver. The Hilbert transform is applied on the linear component obtained from a four-wave spectral decomposition process of the surface elevation, to extract amplitude envelopes and instantaneous phase information, enabling the isolation of critical wave events responsible for extreme structural responses. Each critical wave event is expressed as a sum of focused wave groups using a Gaussian envelope regression methodology, allowing for individual iterative amplitude correction and phase focusing to overcome the challenges of reproducing steep wave events. The corrected focused wave groups are then recombined to create a ‘Hyper-Group’ with accurate spatial and temporal focusing at the desired location. The reproduced event is numerically validated against the original sea-state, demonstrating very good agreement in induced mooring line tension. This methodology provides an efficient framework for generating realistic design waves, supporting targeted numerical and experimental testing of floating offshore wind turbines under extreme conditions.

papers.title: Extended nonlinear theory for water wave modulations under strong winds
papers.abstract: The fourth-order weakly nonlinear theory for modulated wind waves has been derived for a nonlinear-generalized Miles' surface pressure term. The situation of unidirectional waves and a strong wind is considered. The focus is made on the conditions of great and intermediate water depths. Dynamic effects associated with the nonlinear character of the wind–wave interaction have been identified, such as the saturation or intensification of the wind–wave energy exchange, the alteration of the wave and wavegroup shapes including modification of the nonlinear induced flow when the depth is finite, and the complicated picture of the modulational instability. We suggest that a sudden change in wind intensity or direction may contribute to the occurrence of rogue waves due to the wind-dependent bound waves.

papers.title: Effects of tidal-period current variability on vertical fluctuations of the bag-net bottom and landed catch weight in a set-net fishery
Beach scale tidal variations observed from satellite-derived shoreline time series
papers.abstract: Coastal tidal dynamics play a crucial role in a variety of biogeophysical processes, ranging from compound flooding to sediment transport. Satellite altimetry has revolutionized our understanding of ocean tides, but coastal regions remain challenging for satellite altimetry-based observations. In recent years, important efforts have been made to produce shoreline measurements from satellite optical imagery. These datasets raise the question of whether shoreline observations can resolve tidal dynamics at fine coastal scales. Here, we show that shoreline measurements provide fine-scale insights into tidal characteristics, demonstrating variability at beach scales across the Pacific Rim. We explore how both harmonic analysis and response-based methods can be applied to these data to study a range of tidal constituents. Our results are contrasted with in situ measurements and state-of-the-art models as well as with wide-swath satellite observations. We demonstrate that satellite-derived shoreline measurements are a valuable resource for tidal research, particularly for model validation and the study of tidal constituent variability in the coastal zone. Satellite-derived shoreline measurements can provide insights into coastal tidal dynamics and for the validation of models in the coastal zone, according to analyses using shoreline position data from around the Pacific Rim.
